claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (around September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
In the past, having more choices usually meant more complexity, technical debt, and hours of setup.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes.
GeoDeploy provisions consistent environments across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

GeoDeploy's deployment request consists of target geos (with traffic share and data-residency rule of EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape, and constraints (allowed providers, provider count, budget).
In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app never makes judgment calls, Jev never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names, and Pulumi never decides anything.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure when enumerating candidate regions.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy won't run provisioning unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The Pulumi Automation API page exists at /automation/.
Every GeoDeploy run writes plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric you describe; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only ever selects from closed sets, never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument can't happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with constraints and image architecture in a single call.

GeoDeploy asks Jev in one call for a region selection (choice), five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (noul: data residency and capacity), and a fallback region (choice).
GeoDeploy's questions are defined in packages/decide/src/questions.ts and import choice, noul, score from @typesafe-ai/sdk.
TypeSafe's advice for writing rubrics is to "describe situations, not degrees."
GeoDeploy's rubrics each of the 10 levels is a concrete scenario, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" to "In-geo with multiple availability zones..."
The TypeSafeClient in the TypeSafe SDK has a systemOne method taking state and questions, returning answers with fields like selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because ranking weights live in code, GeoDeploy can re-tune the ranking without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy weight profiles: latency-optimized cost 0.13/coverage 0.48/maturity 0.17/sprawl 0.1/arch 0.12; balanced 0.25/0.25/0.2/0.12/0.18; residency-first 0.12/0.12/0.38/0.23/0.15; failure-domain 0.08/0.17/0.48/0.15/0.12.
Every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR), so Jev only decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human); region when stack exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 for region pick, residency, capacity (drop AI path for that geo).
The residency check code is in packages/decide/src/engine.ts and hard-rejects when residencyOk confidence is below 0.95.
Each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic mode comparing prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

In self-driving mode (`geodeploy monitor`), the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.
In self-driving mode, code, not Jev, computes the actual node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it's suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and uses a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency and error rates.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
GeoDeploy is open source today and gates every AI decision on confidence.
GeoDeploy applies hard rejects for data residency.
